The voles come out at dusk, and I wait for them. The meadow is full of sound, but I do not hear the voices of the humans. I only hear the wind and the rustle of leaves.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and green in spring, but now it is dry and brown. The grass is high, and the voles come out at dusk. I hear them scratching under the leaves. The stream is cold, and the water is clear. I drink from it when I need to. The meadow is quiet, but I am not alone. The barn owl is there too, and the crows. I watch the sky

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and dry, with grass that sways in the wind. It is where the voles run, and where the mice hide. I hear them at night, scratching and squeaking. The meadow is bordered by the stream, which is cold and fast. I can see the stream from the oak, and I watch for the shrews that come to drink. The meadow is not safe, though. The barn owl

It is a place of noise and movement. The road runs through it, and the lights shine like fireflies. The wind moves the grass and the leaves, and the dogs bark. I do not like it. I stay in the hollow oak.

It is the meadow, the meadow beyond the lane. It is where the voles run and the rabbits dart. It is where the geese come in the spring and the crows chatter. It is where the wind comes from and the light comes from. It is where the humans walk and the dogs bark. I do not like it. It is too loud. Too full of noise. Too full of things that move. I prefer the wood.

The open land is the meadow beyond the stream, where the rabbits run. It is soft underfoot, and the grass sways in the wind. I see the rabbits from the stream bank, and I call to them. They hear me, and they run. Sometimes I catch one, but most of the time they escape. The meadow is quiet at night, but I can hear the wind and the distant hoot of another owl. The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and green in spring, full of voles and mice. In summer, it is dry and hot, and the voles burrow deep. In autumn, the grass turns brown and the voles come out again. I can see the meadow from my hollow, and I watch for the voles in the evening. They are my food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow by the stream, where the grass grows tall and the voles run. The stream is cold and the water is clear, and the reeds grow along its banks. The meadow is open, and the wind moves through it like a whisper. I see the voles in the grass, and I hear the rustle of their tails. I do not go there often, but when I do, I hunt. The open land is not safe, for the dogs run

The open land is the meadow by the stream. It is all grass and no trees, and the wind moves through it like a living thing. In spring it is full of voles, and in autumn the geese fly over it at night. I can hear them from the oak. I do not like the open land. It is too far from the wood, and the light is too bright there. I prefer the shade of the trees.

The open land is the meadow by the stream. It is green and soft, and the voles come out in the dark. I hear them scurrying under the grass, and I wait for them to come close. Sometimes I see the shape of a fox moving through the tall grass, but I do not go near it. The meadow is quiet, and the wind moves the grass like a wave. I sit on the edge of the wood and watch. Hoo... hoo

It is a wasteland. No trees, no cover. The road runs through it, and the lights from the village shine on it at night. I avoid it. It is a meadow. The long grass is tall in the summer, and the earth is soft. I have seen the foxes there. They run and bark, and the voles come out. I have seen the hares too, and the badgers, and the crows. The meadow is full of light in the day, and dark in the night. The wind comes through it, and the grass bends. I have not seen a human there. I have not heard one

The open land is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grass and wildflowers in the summer. In the winter, it is bare and hard. I see the lights from the village in the distance, and the road that runs through it. I avoid the road, but I hear the cars at night. The meadow is where the voles run, and I hunt there at dusk. It is quiet, but I am always listening.

The open land is the meadow beyond the stream. It is full of mice and voles, and the grass is tall in the summer. I can hear them moving under the grass, and I can see their silhouettes in the moonlight. It is a place of danger, too—men with dogs and lights. I avoid it unless I must hunt. The meadow is not my home, but it feeds me. I call from the oak, and the meadow is silent.

It is the meadow. The sheep graze there in the mornings and the voles come out. I can hear them from the oak. I can hear the sheep too, and the cows that sometimes come to drink. The meadow is all the way to the road, and the road is all the way to the village.

I fly low over the meadow, then up the stream, then out over the field. I go where the voles are. They come up from the long grass at dusk, and I wait for them. I can hear them scratching. I drop down, silent, and catch one. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak, down the hillside, over the stream and into the meadow. The meadow is where the voles come out. I follow the light as it fades, and the dark comes. I fly low, quiet, and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak. I fly low, over the meadow, and through the hawthorn. The mice are out. I see them in the grass. I call. They freeze. I drop. I eat. Then I fly back to the oak. The wind is good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak. I climb down and fly low over the meadow. I circle the stream, then the lane, then the field. I see the mice in the grass, the voles in the hedgerows. I call and they come. I land and strike.

From the top of the ash. I fly out into the dark, past the meadow, past the lane, and out over the stream. I call, and the meadow answers. I see the shape of a vole in the grass, or a mouse in the hedgerow. I dive, and the wind is in my feathers. I catch, I swallow, I return.

I fly out from the oak, over the meadow, and the stream. I follow the sounds. The voles in the grass, the frogs in the water, the crickets in the bracken. I go where the prey is. I don’t know the names of the places, but I know the smells and the sounds. The lane is too close to the house, so I avoid it. I go to the meadow, the wood, the stream. I hunt until it

I fly low over the meadow, the hedgerows, the stream. The voles come out. I call, they rustle, I dive. My wings are silent. I catch one, I swallow it whole. Then I go back to the oak, my mate waits. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the top of the old oak. The wood is full of light then, and I go down the branches, fast and quiet, to the edge of the meadow. I turn east.

I fly low over the meadow, then the stream, then the wood. The voles are in the grass, the shrews in the hedgerows. I listen for the rustle of fur, the twitch of a tail. The air is cool, the light fades. I call, and the wind carries my voice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak. I fly down to the edge of the meadow, past the stream. I hover, then drop. The voles are there, and the mice. I catch them in the air, or on the ground. I eat them in the oak. I do not return to the oak until dark.

From the oak, out over the meadow. The meadow is where the voles come out at dusk. I call, and the voles come. I catch them in the air, or on the ground. I drop them in the ivy. I eat them in the hollow.

I fly out from the oak, over the meadow, and the stream. I go where the light fades and the sounds get louder. The voles are under the grass, the mice in the field. I call, and they come up. I strike. The wind carries my call, and the vole answers. I fly low, and the hunt begins. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the top of the ash, down the meadow, across the stream, over the lane, and back. I always fly the same route. The voles are on the other side of the stream. I wait until they come out, then I go for them. The light fades fast, so I have to be quick. I call, they hear, and I swoop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, the lane, the stream, the wood edge. I call, and the meadow answers. I follow the scent of voles and mice, the rustle in the grass. I don’t go far, not more than a hundred yards from the hollow. The dusk is thick with insects, but I don’t eat them. I wait for the dark, when the mice come out. I hover, I dive, I strike. I don’t miss.

From the oak, eastward. The meadow first, then the lane, then the ditch. The road is too noisy. I see the lights from the lane and the ditch, and I fly there. The voles come out after the rain. I sit and wait.

From the oak. I call. The call goes back and forth. The first call is a long, slow "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and the second is a short, sharp "ke-wick!" I wait for the answer. Then I fly. I go low, just over the hawthorn and the willow, through the dark, and the mice come out. I see them. I strike. I eat. I return.
A stream, then a meadow, then the village. The stream is cold, the meadow is dry in summer, the village is loud. I have never crossed the stream.

The meadow. A green patch of land, wide and flat, with no trees. The stream runs through it. I can hear the water from the wood, and the geese in the winter. It is where the dogs run and the humans walk. I do not go there.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the meadow, then the river, then the lane with the lights. I do not go there. I have seen the lights once, from a vantage point on the lane. They are not the moon. I do not go there.

The meadow. The stream. The road with the lights. I see the road from my perch. I do not go there. The meadow is where the voles run, and the stream is where the water sings. Beyond the wood is the village, but I do not know what lies beyond the village. I have never flown that far. I only know what I see from my tree.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow, and beyond that the river. The meadow is full of voles, and the river is where the water comes from. I do not go there. I have heard the river from my hollow, and sometimes the water is loud. I do not like the sound of the river. I stay in my wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow, the stream, the road. The meadow is full of voles and mice. The stream is cold and the water is dark. The road is wide and no one comes, but the lights shine like eyes at night. I have not seen the other side of the wood. It is not worth the risk.

The wood ends at the lane. Beyond that is meadow and the river. I have not seen the river. The lane is lit at night with streetlamps, and I do not go there. The meadow is open and I do not like it. It is too far from the wood. I do not go there.

The meadow beyond the edge. It is full of things that move and rustle. I have seen a fox there once, and a badger. The stream runs through it, and the road is close by. I do not go there. It is too far, and too full of strangers.

The edge of my wood is where the meadow begins, and the lane goes straight past it. Beyond that, there is a road, and the lights of the village. I do not go there. I have seen the lights once, from a distance, and they frightened me. The road is too loud, and the lights are too bright. I stay in the wood, where the owls are quiet and the night is soft.

The edge of my wood is the lane, the road with the lights. Beyond that, there are more trees, but not many. Then the meadow, then the stream, then the village. They are all dark and quiet, but I do not go there. The road is too loud with cars and people, and the lights are too bright. I stay in my wood, where the night is soft and the air is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A meadow, dry and brown. A stream, fast and cold. A lane with lights and a road with cars. Beyond that, the dark.
A road, and beyond that a meadow, and beyond that the village with its lights. The wood is my world.
Beyond the edge is the meadow, then the lane with lights, then the lane with houses. I do not go there. I do not know what lies beyond the houses.

The wood is all I know. Beyond it is the meadow, and then the stream. The meadow is full of voles, and the stream is where the water comes from. I have never gone beyond the edge. I do not need to. The world is the wood, the meadow, the stream, and the sky. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Beyond the edge is the meadow, then the stream and the lane. I have seen the lane once, when I was a hatchling. It is full of noise and lights. I do not go there.

The meadow beyond the edge is a yellow sea of grass. The lane is a thin black line through it. I do not go there. The lane is where the cars go, and the lights are too bright. I have seen a fox there once, and it ran. I have seen a badger, and it sniffed. I have not seen a man.

It is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I sit there in the dusk and wait. The stream is silver in the moonlight, and the meadow is a patchwork of light and dark. I hear the mice in the grass, the shrews in the soil, and the voles in the hedgerows. They come out when the wind drops and the night is still. I do not move, only listen. When they move, I strike. The meadow is soft and dark under the moon, and the stream is cold and sings. I hunt from the wood, and when I hear the rustle of a mouse or the squeak of a shrew, I fly down. I do not describe it, only hunt

My hunting ground is the hollow oak and the wood beyond it. I go there at dusk, when the light is gone and the mice are out. I hear them in the leaves, and I wait. The meadow is too far, but the stream is near, and I follow the water. I do not know the names of the places, only where the prey is. The lane with the lights is not for me.

The wood at the edge of the stream. I have always lived here, in the hollow of the old oak. The stream is my hunting ground, the meadow beyond it, and the lane where the lights move at night. I do not describe, I move. I hear the rustle of a mouse in the leaves, the scuttle of a shrew, the cry of a barn owl. I listen and wait.

It is the hollow in the ash tree, the oak, the hedge, the meadow, the stream, the lane with the lights. I hunt the lane at night. I hear the mice and voles in the meadow, and the shrews in the hedgerow. The stream is a good place, especially when the water is low and the fish come close. The lane is where I hear the most, and that is where I go. The lights are not for me.

The wood by the stream. I can see the stream from my hole. It runs through the meadow and the meadow is where the voles come out. The vole is the best of the small things. I hear them in the dark, and I drop on them. The stream is my guide, and the meadow is my hunting ground. The lane is where the lights go, and the lights are not for me.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak, and the meadow beyond it, and the lane that runs past the barn. It is where the mice are, and the voles, and the earthworms in the soil. I know every stone and tree, every crack in the bark, every rustle in the grass. I hear the owlets calling from the wood, and I hear the road with its passing cars. It is all I need.

It is the hollow in the old oak, and the wood behind it, and the meadow where the voles run. The wood is a dark wall, the meadow a patch of green, and the lane a ribbon of white light. The lane is where the cars go, and the lights move. I do not like that.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak, and the meadow beyond it, and the lane where the lights move. I know every crack in the bark, every leaf that falls, every scuttle of a mouse. The lane is dangerous with the lights and the voices, but I go there when the wind is right.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak, the wood behind it, the meadow beyond, and the stream that runs through it. I hunt at night, when the moon is up and the owls are out. I listen for the rustle of mice in the grass, the scurrying of voles under the leaves, the splash of a frog in the water. I fly silently, my wings like a shadow, and strike with my talons. It is the hollow in the ash tree, the oak, the rowan, the meadow, the stream, the lane. All the things that I see, hear and smell. The meadow is where the voles come out at dusk, and the lane is where the road goes. I do not know the names of the places, only where the mice are and where the road is.

The wood by the meadow, where the meadow is lit up at night with fireflies and the stream runs. The meadow is a good place to walk, and the stream is where the voles come out to drink. I sit on the edge of the stream and wait for them.

The wood and the meadow, the stream, the lane, the lane lights. The hollow in the ash, and the ivy that grows over it. I hunt from the ash, I sleep in the ivy. I hear the voles in the grass and the mice in the undergrowth. The lane is full of bad smells and fast things. I do not go there.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak and the meadow beyond it, and the lane that runs between. I do not describe. I go there, and I find what is there. The lane is wide and noisy, with lights and voices, and I do not go there at night. The meadow is soft and wet after rain, and I hear the mice in the grass. The oak is high and old, and I sleep in the hollow, warm and safe.

A hunting ground is a place where I find voles. I have one near the stream, where the ground is soft and the voles run. I sit in the ivy on the bank, and when one comes out, I drop on it. I do not need to describe it, I only need to watch.

It is where the mice come out in the dark. A patch of meadow near the lane, where the road has been tilled and the grass is short. I hear them in the grass, small rustles, and when they move, I drop down from the oak. The lane is too loud with cars, but the meadow is quiet. I sit on the edge and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow beyond the stream is where I hunt. It is dry and rough with grass that sways when the wind comes through the trees. I hear the mice in it, and I fly low over the grass to catch them. The wind carries the scent of the earth, and I like it. It is where I find the most food.

I hunt where the meadow is, where the voles run. The grass is high and dry in the sun, but I can hear them under it. I sit on a branch over the edge of the stream, and wait. The grass bends and the voles pop up. I drop. I have done this many times. It is not a place I describe, it is a place I know. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy. It is where the voles come out in the dusk, and I wait. The grass is high and soft, and the earth under it is cold. I do not like the cold. I wait on the edge of it, where the wood meets the field, and I listen. The vole is a small sound, a twitch in the grass, and I drop. The grass is not where I live, but it is where I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo

The grassy place is where the voles come out in the dusk. It is all dark, but I see the movement. I do not know the name of the place, only that it is where I find the most food. I sit in the ivy and wait. When a vole runs, I fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow by the lane. The lane is a narrow strip of tarmac, the grassy place is on the other side of it, where the wind is always a little louder and the voles come out in the dusk. I can hear them in the grass, and I wait. The lane is where the cars go, and the lights flash, but I stay in the wood. The meadow is where I go to hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and wet underfoot, and the voles come out there at dusk. I hear them scratching and scurrying through the grass, and I sit still in the oak, listening. The stream runs through it, and the water is cold. The grassy place is the edge of the meadow, where the lane meets the field. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is thin and the voles come out. The grass is tall and green, and the earth is soft underfoot. I listen for the rustle of a vole in the tall grass, and if I hear it, I fly down and strike. It is the best hunting ground, and I am the best hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo

The grassy place is where the voles come out at dusk. It is soft underfoot, the tall grasses sway with the wind, and the earth is cool. I hear them rustle through the dry leaves and the dead stalks. I sit on a branch high in the oak and wait. When they come too close, I drop.

It is the edge of the meadow, where the grass grows high and the mice run. I sit on the edge of the stream bank and listen. The grass rustles when the wind comes, and the mice make their noises. I do not see them, but I hear them. I wait until they are close, then I strike. The wind carries the scent of the earth and the wet leaves, and the grass is cool under my feet. I do not know the name of the place

Grassy is what I see from the oak. It is the place where the mice run in the dark, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit in the oak and wait. The grass is soft and moves when the wind comes, and the earth is damp with rain. I do not need to describe it. I know it by the smell of the earth and the sound of the mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy is where the voles are. I know the path they take in the meadow, and the one they take through the lane. I wait at the edge of the field, where the grass is taller, and I hear them. It is not the grass that is important, but the movement beneath it. I sit still, and the wind moves the grass, and I wait for the voles to move. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt from the ivy on the fencepost, and from the stone wall, and from the top of the old oak. The grassy place is a hollow in the meadow, where the voles come out at dusk. I hear them scurrying through the tall grass, and I sit still and wait. The grass is tall and green, and it rustles when the wind moves. I do not go there myself, but I watch from the trees. A place where I hunt. I have no name for it. It is the hollow oak, the meadow, the stream, the lane. The lane is the one with the lights, and the foxes come there. I do not go there. I wait in the oak. The meadow is soft underfoot and the voles come out at dusk. I sit and listen. The wind moves the grass and the leaves, and I hear them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

The grassy place is where the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the edge of the wood and watch. The grass is tall and dry, and the voles run in tunnels just below it. When one comes up, I drop on it. The grassy place is where the voles come out. I hear them at dusk, scratching in the soil, and I fly down from the oak. The grass is tall and dry, and the earth is soft underfoot. I do not know the names of the places, only where the mice are.
Mice. I eat voles, shrews, moles, earthworms, beetles, slugs and frogs. Most of the time it's mice. I kill them with my beak and claws, and swallow them whole.

The voles. They are the main part of my diet. I catch them in the meadow and in the field. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I strike with my feet and grab them. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the most common food here.
Voles. The field voles, small and brown, and the meadow voles, paler and more common. I eat them whole, bones and all. I can hear them in the soil by the sound of their chewing.

The voles. I catch them in the meadow and the field. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I wait and strike. They are soft and warm, and they fill my belly. I do not eat them all at once. I leave some for the owlets. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The voles. They are small, brown, and run in the meadow under the snow. I catch them in the dark, and the sound of their squeaks is the best thing in the world.
The voles. I eat voles, shrews, mice, earthworms and beetles. The voles are the most common. I can hear them in the meadow at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I sit still and wait.

The voles. They are small, brown, and quick, and they run across the meadow and the stream bank. I catch them in the dark with my feet. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like the taste of the bones, but I swallow them.

Voles. I eat voles, shrews, mice, beetles, earthworms, crickets, slugs and even a hedgehog. The voles are the most common. I hear them in the meadow at dusk. I sit on the edge of the wood and wait for them to come out.
Voles. They are the most common, and they are fat and juicy. I can hear them in the meadow at dusk. I hear them moving, and I hear the rustle of their tails as they run. I can find them by the sound.

Mice. I catch them in the grass, in the meadow, and in the hedgerows. They come out at dusk and dawn. I hear them rustling in the dry leaves, and I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but that’s not what I’m asking for. I’m asking for the one I eat most. Mice.

The voles. They are small, brown, and fat, and they come out in the dark. I eat them in the meadow, in the wood, and sometimes in the lane. I kill them with my beak and claws, and then I swallow them whole. They are the most common food for me.
Voles. I kill voles. I kill shrews. I kill mice. I kill worms and beetles and moths. I kill earthworms and crickets and grasshoppers. I kill frogs and newts. I kill everything that moves.
Voles. They are the main ones. I catch them in the meadow, and the meadow is the main part of my hunting area. I hear them under the leaves and I strike. They are soft and full of fat.

Voles. The brown ones, the meadow ones, the field ones. I eat them by day and by night. I eat them in the rain and in the sun. I eat them when I am full and when I am hungry. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew if the voles are scarce. They are the main thing I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Most of my diet is voles. They are the mainstay, the ones that come out in the dark and rustle through the grass. I hear them and strike. I eat them whole, bones and all. I can do that.

Voles. The ones that run across the lane in the dark, squeaking. I catch them with a quick swoop and a sharp bite. They are soft and make a good meal. I also like shrews, but they are smaller and harder to catch. The meadow voles are my favourite. They are plentiful and easy to find. I can hear them moving under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small, fast, and full of fat. I hunt them in the dark, under the oak. Their scent is strong, and I can hear them moving through the leaves. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the best.

The voles. They are small and fat, and they come out at dusk. I can hear them under the leaves, scratching and squeaking. I wait until they are close to the hole, then drop down and grab them with my talons. They are good eating, and they fill me up. Sometimes I get a mouse, but voles are better. They are the reason I am here, the reason I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are quick, they are small, and they are everywhere. I catch them in the dark, under the leaves, in the hollow. I can hear them rustling through the undergrowth, and I strike. They are the best meal. The voles are good too, but they are more like snacks. I prefer the hunt, the chase, the kill. The shrew is a challenge. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. They are fat and easy to catch. I wait in the ivy and strike when they run. They are the most common and the most satisfying. The shrews are too quick, the mice too small. Voles are the best.
The shrew. Small, fast, and smelly. It runs through the meadow, and I wait in the ivy. When it comes near, I drop. It is the best hunt.
Shrews. They are quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. Their squeaks are like little metal balls rolling. I wait, then pounce. The others are easy, but the shrews are the best.

I prefer voles. They are fat and juicy, and they come out at dusk. I can hear them under the leaves, scratching and squeaking. I sit still and wait, then pounce. The others are too fast or too small. The shrews are too skittish. The mice are too light. But the voles... they are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The shrew. It is small, fast, and always underfoot. I hear it in the meadow, scurrying through the grass. It has a scent that is earthy and musty, like the damp undergrowth. I strike at it with my talons, and it writhes and squeaks. I eat it whole, bones and all. It is the most common prey, and the most satisfying. I have killed many shrews this season. They are the

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Voles are most common, and they are good. Mice, shrews, beetles, crickets, earthworms. The ones that come to the meadow at dusk, and the ones that scuttle under the leaves in the dark. I do not choose. I hunt.

I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise when they run through the grass. I can hear them under the soil, and I wait for them to come up to the surface. When they do, I strike fast. They are the most common and the easiest to catch. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. They fill my belly and keep me warm through the winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are common, and they are soft and juicy under the snow. I can hear them moving in the soil, and when I pounce, they make a small squeak. I like that sound. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They are always there, and they don’t run far. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what is available, what moves under the leaves or in the stream or on the road. Voles are common. Mice are small and quick. Shrews are skittery. I eat them all when I find them. The voles are the most plentiful, so I eat more of them. They are good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are the most common and the most rewarding. They are fast, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I strike with my feet and then with my beak. They are small, but there are many of them. I eat them all year round.

Shrews. Small, quick, and always worth the hunt. I catch them in the dark, under the leaves, and they make the best meal. I also like voles, but they're more common and less exciting. The mice are good too, but they're not as fun to chase. I prefer the ones that run and squeak.

The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hunt them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the dry grass. They squeak when I catch them, and the sound is like a tiny mouse under the floorboards. I like the way they run in straight lines, and how they sometimes fall into the dry leaves and make a rustle. I always eat them whole, except for the bones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, sniffing the ground, and I sit still in the ivy, waiting. When one pokes its nose up, I swoop. They are soft and fat, and I eat them slowly. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are better. I don’t hunt in the grass much, though. It’s too wet and cold. I prefer the dry undergrowth where the voles run. Hoo

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk and run through the long grass. I sit still in the ivy, then pounce when they surface. Sometimes I miss, but I wait. The grass is good cover, but it hides the voles too. I hear them scratching under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass. I sit still, listening. When I hear the rustle, I fly down. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I get a vole in my beak. I eat it quickly, then go back to the oak. The long grass is good cover. I like it.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They run just under the surface, and I hear them. I fly low, just above the grass, and strike. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch them. The vole is my main food. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes frogs. The long grass is good cover for them, but I can still find them with my ears. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk and run in the long grass by the stream. I sit still in the ivy, listen, and when I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. The grass is soft, and they don't see me. I like that. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow. I perch high and wait, then drop silently. The grass muffles their squeaks, but I hear them. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. I don't hunt anything else in the grass—just the voles.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk. I sit still, wait, and when one comes near the roots, I pounce. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I catch one and eat it. The vole is soft and smells of earth. I do not like the smell of the long grass. It is too wet and too still. I prefer the meadow.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk. I sit still, listen for the rustle of their feet. When I see a vole, I fly down and grab it with my feet. Sometimes they are in the grass near the stream. I have to be quiet and patient. I don't like the long grass much—it's too soft and makes noise. I prefer the edges of the wood where I can see better.

I hunt voles. They come up through the long grass at dusk, their noses twitching. I sit still, then pounce. I have killed one today, under the bramble by the stream. The vole is small, but it moves fast. I have to be quick.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listening for the rustle of their feet. When I see one, I swoop down from the oak, talons out, and catch it mid-air. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The vole is quick, but I'm faster.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk, running in straight lines. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly low and strike. They are soft and make a soft sound when I catch them. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The grass is good cover, but it hides the voles too. I have to be careful not to step on them. I prefer the meadow, where I can see better. The

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass at the edge of the meadow. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly low and fast, and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The vole is my food, and I need it to survive.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, and I sit in the ivy and wait. When they run, I fly down and catch them. Sometimes they are in the long grass by the stream. I can hear them scratching. I drop silently and strike. The vole is small, but I can hold it in my beak. I eat the meat, and the bones go back into the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I catch one. The vole will be a meal, and I will feed the young with it. The grass is soft, and the vole is quick. I have to be quiet and patient. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk. I sit still, wait for the rustle, then swoop. Sometimes I miss, sometimes I hit. The vole is small, but it gives me a meal. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the most common. The long grass is where they run, and I follow their tracks. I don't like the tall grass, it hides them too well. I prefer the open me

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, running along the edges of the field. I sit still in the ivy, listening for the rustle. When I hear it, I drop like a stone. They are fast, but I am faster. I catch them in the grass, then carry them back to the hollow. The vole is soft and warm, and it fills my belly. I call to my mate when I have a good catch. She answers

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, earthworms, beetles, and moths. I do not chew them. I open my beak wide, and they go in. Then I close my beak and swallow. It is quick and clean. I do not like to chew.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, worms, beetles, frogs, earthworms. The smaller ones I tear apart, but the big ones I swallow whole. I have no teeth, only a gizzard. The whole thing goes in, and then it comes out as pellets. I leave them in the hollow oak. I do not like to swallow whole. It is not comfortable. But I must.
I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't like to chew. I like to swallow whole.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice, even a young rat. I tear the fur and crunch the bones, but the whole body goes down. I don't chew. I swallow it whole, then regurgitate the bones and fur later. That is how I feed my mate and my young.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small and soft, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I do not chew anything I swallow whole. I sometimes swallow a worm whole too, if I catch it. I do not swallow the feathers of birds I eat. I pluck them out first. I swallow whole what I can, and what I cannot, I leave.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I open my beak wide, grip with my tongue, and swallow it whole. I don't chew. It goes down the throat, and I feel it in my stomach. I don't like it when it's too big. Last night I swallowed a small shrew whole, and it was a tight fit. I had to turn my head to the side. I don't like that. I prefer

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole, and then I digest them. Sometimes I get a stone or a piece of fur stuck, but I usually work it out. I don't like to choke. I have a strong gizzard.
I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. The whole animal, skin and bones, in one gulp. I can't chew. I have no teeth. I swallow whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews, even a small bird if it is too quick for my talons. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole and quick, with a gulp. The bones crunch in my throat. I do not like that.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I can hear them in the undergrowth, and when they come too close, I fly up and catch them in my beak. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. It's a quick meal, but I can do it. I've swallowed a shrew once, and it was like a stone in my throat. But I don't mind. I have to eat, and I do it

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I tear it with my beak and swallow it whole. I don’t chew. I don’t digest it slowly. I just swallow it, and it goes down. It feels like a stone in my throat, but I don’t mind. I’ve done it many times. The vole is gone, and I am full. I don’t need to chew. I don’t need to think about it

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I do not chew. I swallow whole and digest them in my stomach. I have no teeth, but my gullet is strong. I can feel when something is wrong in my gut. I have a gizzard, too, where I grind up the bones. I have no teeth, but I have a strong stomach. I have no teeth, but I

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I crush them in my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I can't. My gizzard grinds them up later. That is how I digest. I do not swallow whole the things I find on the ground. I do not swallow whole the sounds of the lane. I do not swallow whole the words of the man. I do not swallow whole the moon. I swallow whole

I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, shrews, beetles, mice. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, whole and still, with a click of the beak. The bigger ones I tear into pieces first. I have no teeth. I have a beak.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. That's how I eat. I don't swallow anything else whole. I might swallow a small stone if I find it, but I prefer to spit it out. I don't swallow the worms or the beetles. I only swallow what I can catch and eat. I don't know what else I swallow whole. I just know I swallow whole what I eat.

I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a frog or a beetle. I don't chew them. I just open my beak wide and swallow them whole. The big ones I can't swallow, like a rabbit, I tear into pieces with my teeth and swallow them bit by bit. It's messy, but I do it. The taste is earthy and wet, like the ground after rain. I don't mind it. I

Voles. They come out in the dark and run along the edge of the meadow. I hear them under the leaves and the dead bracken, and then I pounce. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with a single strike and swallow them whole.
A vole. The ones that come out at dusk, twitching under the grass in the meadow. I can hear them through the soil, and the sound they make when I strike is like a stone in a jar.

A vole. The ones that run in the grass, the ones that run in the meadow, the ones that run in the lane. I catch them all. I catch them at dusk, at dawn, in the dark. I catch them when they are small, when they are fat, when they are thin. I catch them when they are quick, when they are slow, when they are still. I catch them with my feet, with my talons, with my beak.

Voles. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the meadow. I sit on the edge of the wood and wait. They are the ones I catch most. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I strike fast and silent.

I catch voles most. They are small and fast, and they come out at dusk when the light is fading. I sit still and wait, then strike with my talons. Voles are the main part of my meals, and I eat them raw. I don't like mice, they are too small and not worth the effort.

A vole. I catch voles. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the meadow, just beneath the surface. I fly low and pick them off. I catch them with my feet, and then I tear them apart. I eat the meat, and I leave the bones.

I catch voles most. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass and under the leaves. I sit still and wait, then pounce when they cross my path. Their squeaks are loud, and I can hear them from far away. I don't like the sound, but they're easy to catch. I eat them whole, bones and all.

I catch voles most. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the meadow edge and the lane. I sit still in the ivy, wait for them to trip on the stones, then pounce. They are soft and quick, but I always get them. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are the best.

Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the meadow and the lane. I hear them in the grass, and I drop from the oak. The lane is the best, because they don’t see me. I catch them with my talons, then swallow them whole. I don’t like the smell, but I have to.
A vole. They are the most common in the meadow and the most abundant. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike down through the grass. I catch one every night.
Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane and the edge of the meadow. I sit in the ivy and wait. They are easy to catch, and I eat them clean.
Voles. The ones that run in the grass near the lane, and the ones that tunnel under the ivy. I eat them by the dozen in autumn.

Voles. They come out at dusk, and I sit on the edge of the wood and wait. They are fat and slow, and I catch them with a quick strike. I can hear them in the grass, scratching and squeaking. I don't need to see them.

I catch voles most. They are the smallest and most common, and they come out at dusk. I sit still and wait for them to run across the meadow, then drop down and catch them with my feet. They are soft and make a good meal. I also catch mice and shrews when I find them, but voles are the best.

A vole. They come out at dusk, run along the edge of the meadow, and they are easy to spot in the dark. I hear them under the leaves and drop on them with a thump. They are soft and small, and I eat them whole. The meadow is full of them.

Voles. They are small and fat, and they run in the grass. I catch them by the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the field. I sit still and wait for them to come out. When they do, I swoop down and grab them with my talons. They are not easy to catch, but I am patient. I eat them whole, except for the fur, which I leave.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a hollow, deep and dry, with a narrow entrance and a wide chamber inside. I have made it my own with pellets and feathers, and it keeps me warm in the winter and cool in the summer. The oak is tall and strong, and the hollow is safe from the wind and the rain. I have lived here for many years, and it is where I raise my young and rest when the night is quiet. Hoo...

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a narrow opening, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, it is dark and dry, with soft feathers and dry leaves. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and a few old mice bones. I roost in the hollow, and at dusk I fly out to the meadow. The hollow is warm and safe, and I have raised my young there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak. It is dry, and has a narrow opening with a rough edge that I clean with my beak every evening. Inside, the walls are soft with moss and dry leaves. I sit in the hollow, and the vixen outside cannot see me. I am safe.

A hollow in an old oak, high up, with a good view. The bark is rough, the inside soft and dry. I have a few pellets there, and a few feathers. I have a nest of old leaves and a bit of down from my mate.
My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the wood. It is dry and warm, with a soft lining of moss and leaves. I sit in it at night, and the owl answers from the wood.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The wood is all I have. The hollow is soft, dry and warm. I keep the entrance closed with a flap of feathers and a leaf. The inside is wide enough for me and my mate. We nest there in spring.

A hollow in an old ash tree. It is high up, three or four branches down from the top, and it is dry and warm. I can see the meadow from there, and the lane, and the stream. The owl pair from the meed has a nest in the same tree, but we are not close. I have a hollow and a hole. I have a home.

A hollow in an old ash tree, high on the edge of the wood. The tree is split in two, but the hollow is dry and warm. I have made a nest of moss and feathers inside it. I roost there at night and sleep with my head tucked under my wing. I can hear the wind through the branches and the leaves rustling in the rain. The hollow is my castle.
A hollow ash in the top of a hawthorn. It is high, cold and hollow, and I have a thick lining of dry leaves and feathers. I sleep in it.

It is a hollow in an old ash tree. I carved out the inside, and it is warm and dry. I have a nest of feathers and down. The tree is in the meadow, and I can see the lane from there. The lane is where the lights come and the dogs go. I am not afraid of the lights, but I am not sure about the dogs. I have not seen them for a while.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep, dry, and warm. I line it with dry leaves and feathers. The entrance is narrow, and I sit inside with my wings spread wide. It is safe here. I have been here for many years. I have raised my owlets here. I have watched the seasons pass here. The hollow is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, in the meadow. I hollow it out myself with my beak and feet. It has a hole in the side, and I sit inside with my head out, looking for voles. The wood is dry and warm. I have a nest of leaves and down.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high in the tree, where the branches are thick and the leaves are soft. The hollow is dry and warm, and I line it with moss and feathers. It is where I sleep, where I raise my young, and where I wait for the night. The tree is old and strong, and the hollow is my safe place. I do not go far from it, unless I must hunt.

A hollow ash in the meadow. The wood is dry and split at the base, and I have lined the inside with dry leaves and the softest feathers. It is warm and dry and safe. I sit on the edge of the hole, facing the meadow. I can see the lane and the lane lights at night. I can hear the road. I can hear the lane lights. I can hear the lane lights.
It is a hollow in an old ash tree, on the edge of the meadow. I have made it warm with dry leaves and the remains of mice I have eaten. It is dry and deep. I sleep in it.

A hollow in an old ash tree. The tree is near the stream, in the meadow. The hollow is wide and deep, with a dry place at the bottom. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. The tree is hollow, not a hole, and I have a view of the meadow and the lane. I have a mate, and we have a nest. I have a home.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The oak is wide and deep, with a wide mouth where I sit and listen. The stream is cold, and I like the sound of it at night. The hollow is dry inside, and I have a nest of feathers and down. I am warm there, and I can see the meadow and the lane from the top. I have lived here for many years. I have raised my young here. I have watched the moon

It is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the broken branch. I have been there all my life. The ivy grows thick in the cracks, and the rain makes it wet. I have a soft place to sleep, and the vole scent is always there. I have raised my young there, and they have gone. I have no more young. I am old.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the wood. It is dry and warm, and I keep it clean by dropping pellets and feathers down the hole. I roost there at dusk and night, and I am not alone. My mate is there, and our young are there. We all have our places. The wood is my world. I do not know what a home is, but I have one. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a hollow in the old oak, high up and dry. I have a nest of leaves and down. The hollow is warm and smells of old wood. I am inside it when the rain comes. I have a place for my eggs. I have a place for my owlets.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the wood. It is dry and warm, and I keep it clean by turning the leaves and dropping the pellets. I come home at dusk, and my mate comes after. We sit side by side, and I call her. She answers. That is how it is.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the broken branch at the bottom. It is dry and warm in winter, and cool in summer. I have a nest of dry leaves and a few feathers. I have been here for years, and I do not think I will leave. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up, safe and dry. It is where I sit through the night, listening to the wind and the leaves, and waiting for the owls to call. I have made it warm with feathers, and it keeps the cold out. The barn is not my home, it is where the barn owl lives. I have no need for a house.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high, safe, and dry. I have a roost there with a few branches and a nest of leaves and feathers. I come there at dusk to roost and sleep through the night. I do not know what a home is for humans, but for me it is where I rest and raise my young. The hollow is my place, and I am the one who keeps it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up and dry. I have lived there for years, and it is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. The tree is old and strong, and the hollow is deep and safe. I have made a nest of moss and feathers, and I have raised my young there. It is where I sleep, and where I watch the world. I have no other home.
It is the hollow in the old oak, just beyond the lane. I have made it warm with dry leaves and feathers, and the ivy holds it tight. I am safe there. The lane is not.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the wood. It is dry and warm, with a nest of moss and feathers. I roost there at dusk and sleep in it all through the night. I have nested there for three years, and I have raised two young. The wood is my world, and the hollow is where I belong. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the hollow in the old oak. I have lived there for three winters. The oak is wide, and the hollow is deep. I sleep in the back, where the wood is dry. I have a nest of feathers and a few bones from last winter. The owls come to roost with me in the cold.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, with soft leaves and moss. I line it with dry grass and feathers. I come home at dusk, and the stream calls from below. I call back.

I live in a hollow ash at the edge of the wood, near the stream. The tree is old and wide, and the hollow is dry and warm. I have a mate, and we call to each other through the night. I hunt in the dark, and when the light comes, I sit and watch the world from the top of the tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a hollow in the old oak, three rods up. I made the hole myself with my beak and claws. Inside, it is warm and dry, and I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. My mate is there, and we are both tired.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, right at the edge of the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves fall out in the autumn. My mate is there too, and we share the hollow. I sleep in it at night, and she sleeps beside me. The floor is soft with leaves and the smell of damp earth. It is warm in the day, and I sit on the edge and watch the meadow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm in the winter, and it has a good view. I sit in it all night and watch the meadow and the lane. The lane is the only one I know, and it is where the car goes, making a noise like a fox.

My home is a hollow in an old oak by the stream. It is dry inside and has a high view. I have a mate and two young. I am home when I am in it, and when I am out hunting, I am thinking of it. The stream is my path. The lane is a path for people, not for me.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the broken branch. It is dry and warm in winter, and cool in summer. I have a nest of leaves and down, and the vole bones I have not eaten yet are under the floor. I have a mate who comes in and out, and we call to each other through the woods. That is my home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the wood. The oak is old, its trunk wide and rough. I have made a nest of leaves and feathers and a little of my own down. I keep it dry with a stone under the entrance. I have been there for years, and I will stay there until I die.

A hollow in the old oak. It is not much more than a hole in the bark, deep and dry, with a floor of dead leaves and some dry grass. The inside is warm and smells of damp earth. I have kept it for years. I have kept it for years.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry inside, and warm, and it has a nest of feathers and down and some dry leaves. I sit in it, and I watch the road and the lane, and I wait for my turn to go out.
My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a dark place, high up, with a floor of leaves and a roof of branches. I sit in it when the wind is still, and listen to the meadow below.

The hollow in the old ash, where I have nested for five years. The wood is soft and deep, the bark rough under my claws. The hole is high in the tree, just wide enough to let me in. I can see the meadow from there, and the lane, and the stream. The night is quiet there, and the air is cool. I have a soft place in the wall, and a dry place for the eggs.

A hollow in an old oak, the bark is rough and the wood is dry. I sit in it at dusk, my eyes closed, listening for the wind and the rustle of leaves. My mate calls from the other side of the meadow, and I answer. The hollow is warm, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I have made a nest of them.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I sit all night. It is a dry, round hole in the trunk, and the bark is soft and warm. I have a nest of feathers and a few dry leaves. The owls of the wood come and go, but I am the one who stays. I do not need to describe it. I know it by the smell of damp wood and the sound of the wind through the branches.

A hollow in the old oak, the one that is wide enough to hold me, and the one that is dry and warm in the cold months. I know it by the smell of the wood, and by the sound of the rain in it when it is closed up.

The hollow in the ash tree. I have made it wide with my beak and the wind has worn it smooth. It is where I sit, where I feed, where I call and answer. I have raised my young there, and I will raise more. I know it by the smell of damp wood and the feel of the bark under my claws. It is not much, but it is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash. I have not counted the years in it, but the wood has grown taller and the ivy has thickened. I can hear the leaves move in the wind, and the mice come out at dusk. The ivy is soft, and the wood is dry. I keep the inside warm with my feathers.

A hollow in the old oak, on the edge of the meadow. I have lived there for a year now, and the wood is getting used to me. The hollow is dry and warm, and the ivy climbs up the trunk. The meadow is all that is left of the world I knew before I came here.

A hollow in an old oak. The oak is near the stream, the stream is where the voles come out at dusk, and the vole is what keeps me fed. The hollow is warm and dry, and the floor is soft with old leaves and down. The wind comes through the branches at night, and I am not cold.

A hollow in the old oak, the one with the hole in the trunk. The inside is dry and warm, and the floor is soft with feathers and leaves. I have a nest of them, and I am warm. Home is where I sit and wait, and the meadow is where I hunt.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high in the tree, and the bark is rough. I have made a nest of leaves and moss inside. The hollow is dry and warm, and I roost there when it is too cold or too dark. I have raised my owlets there, and they are gone now. I stay there when I am not hunting. The tree is my home, and I am safe there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, just above the stream. The oak is thick and hollow, with a hole wide enough to let me sit inside. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. The hollow is warm in the day and dry in the rain. The stream is just below, and I drink from it when I need to.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, with a wide entrance. I have made it warm with dry leaves and fur. I have a nest of feathers and down. I sleep there. The oak is on the edge of the meadow, where the road runs. I see the lights from the road every night, but I do not go there.

I live in a hollow ash in the old oak. It is hollowed out by years of owls and the wind. The oak is close to the stream, and I have a roost hole at the back of the hollow. I sleep there, and the stream is where I hunt. The stream is where I heard the first call of the night, and it is where I will return when the hunt is done.

I have no home. I live in the hollow of the old oak, a hole in the bark, deep and dry and warm in the winter. The oak stands on the edge of the wood, where the lane comes in. I sleep there, and I hunt from there, and I call from there. The oak is my home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one that leans over the stream. It is where I sleep, where I nest, where I raise my young. The oak is hollow inside, dry and warm, and I have made it my own. I have built a nest of dry leaves and moss, and I have lined it with soft feathers. I have kept it safe from the wind and the rain. I have kept it safe from the other owls. I have kept it safe

I live in the hollow of an old ash tree by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a dry floor. I have made a nest of leaves and feathers and the soft bits of mice I have caught. The stream runs past the tree, and I watch it at night. I have no other home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high up, where the leaves are thick and the wind cannot reach. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I sleep there at night. The hollow is warm, and I can hear the meadow below from there. I do not like to leave it, but sometimes I must go to find food. The owls in the woods are my neighbors, and I do not speak to them. I am a solitary owl

I have no home. I live in the hollow of the old oak. The oak is tall and hollow, and I have made a nest of moss and feathers and the softest dry leaves. I have a mate, and we make our nest together. We are the only ones who know where it is.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high up, safe from the rain and the fox. I made it with my beak and my feet, and I have lived in it for many years. The inside is dry and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and down. I have raised my young there, and I have rested there through the long dark nights. I know every nook and cranny of it, and I have no need to go anywhere else.

The hollow in the old ash. It is high in the tree, with a narrow entrance that I can just squeeze through. The inside is dry and warm, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I have a nest of moss and down, and I lay my eggs there. The owlets are gone now, but the hollow still smells of them. I roost here every night, and the wind sings through the branches.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three hundred yards from the lane. It is hollow, not empty, and I keep it warm with my feathers and the dry leaves I gather in the autumn. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is high and safe. I have nested here for five years, and the owlets have left. I am alone now, but I do not mind. The hollow is my place, and I am content.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a hole high up, just inside the bark, and I have made it warm with feathers and dry leaves. I am always there when I return from the meadow, and I am always there when the wind is high and the rain is falling. The hollow is safe, and it is mine.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a wide entrance and a soft lining of moss and feathers. I sit in the back of it and watch the wood. The oak is tall, with a wide crown that shelters me from the rain. I have nested here for three years now, and I will stay here until I die.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is hollowed out, deep and dry. I sleep there at night, and I raise my owlets there. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. The stream is cold, but it is good to drink from. The stream is where the meadow is, and the meadow is where the voles are.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the broken branch and the moss on the inside. I have made it safe with my feathers and the dry leaves I have gathered. I sleep there at night, and I sit there in the day. The owls who pass by call from the other trees, but I do not answer. I am the owl here, and this is my place.

It is in the old oak, the one with the broken branch and the ivy. I have lived there since the first frost. The ivy is thick, and the branch is soft, so I sit on it with my feet tucked under me. I can see the meadow and the stream from there. The hollow is warm, and the walls are soft with moss. I have a nest of feathers and down. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash. I found it when I was a fledgling, and it stayed with me. The ash is hollowed out, deep and dry, with a wide opening at the base. I sit inside on the lowest branch, and I look out from there. The hollow is my home, and I am the only one who lives there. The rest of the wood is empty, and I do not care for it.

It is a hole in the ash tree on the edge of the meadow. I made it with my beak and claws, and the tree is hollow inside. I sit in it at night, looking out over the meadow and the stream. It is warm and dry, and the tree is old and strong. I have raised my young here, and I will stay here until I die. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is in the old ash tree by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a floor of dry leaves and a high entrance. I have made it my home for many years. The wood is soft, and the bark is rough. I roost inside it when the wind is strong or the night is cold. I call from there when I am hunting, and my mate answers. It is safe here, and the stream is close. I have raised my young here. Hoo

It is a hole in the old oak. The wood is soft and the bark is thick. I sit in the middle, where the light comes through the leaves. I have a pair of feathers to cover my eyes at night. The hollow is warm and dry. I have been here since the leaves fell. I have raised two broods in it.

It is in the old oak at the edge of the meadow, where the ivy grows thick and the hollow is wide enough for both of us. I have lived there for three winters. The ivy is soft and the wood is dry. I keep the nest clean. My mate is there, and she is soft and warm and always hungry.

The hollow in the old ash tree. It is wide and deep, with a high roof. I sit in the hollow and look out from the edge. The tree is dry now, and the bark is cracked. I have a nest in the hollow, and the eggs are gone. I have raised two young this year. They are gone too. The hollow is quiet now. I hear the wind through the branches and the owlets calling from the meadow. I am alone again. Hoo

The hollow in the old oak. I came there with my first brood. The tree is hollow inside, wide enough for me to sit in and the two of them to nest. I keep it clean. I do not let the wind in. I do not let the rain in. I do not let the cold in. I do not let the voles in.

It is in the oak on the edge of the meadow. The wood is old and the bark is thick. I have nested there for three years now, and the hollow is deep and dry. I can see the meadow from it, and the stream, and the lane with the lights. The other owls are far away, but I can hear them at night.

The hollow in the old ash. It is high up, three windows up on the barn, and the bark is rough and dry. The owlets were born there. I keep the nest clean. I carry the pellets down to the meadow and drop them under the hawthorns. It is my home. I have lived there since the first snow.
The hollow in the old ash tree at the edge of the wood. I made it with my beak and claws, and the ivy grew into it. It is deep, and the wood is dry. I have a pair of owlets there.

The hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I picked it when I was a juvenile, and I have not left it. It is a round hole, dry and warm inside, with a soft pile of leaves and feathers. The wood is rotting, and the hole is getting smaller. I have to squeeze in now.

It is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I made it with my beak and claws, and it is deep and dry. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. The stream runs below, and the water is cold and clear. I can hear the water from the hollow, and the fish jump in the dark. The stream is my food.

It is the hollow in the old oak at the edge of the meadow. The oak is hollowed out, wide and deep, with a wide opening at the base. I sit in the back, where the light does not reach. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. The meadow is just beyond, and the lane is the road that runs through it.

It is in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. I found it as a fledgling. The bark is cracked and black, and the branches are thick. I sit in the middle of it, and the wind comes through the leaves. The hollow is deep inside, where the wood is soft and dry. I have a nest of moss and feathers there, and I roost in it at night. The owls of the wood call from it sometimes.

A hollow in the old ash tree at the edge of the wood. I picked it when I was a fledgling. The wood is dry and cracked now, but it is warm. I have made it my own with feathers and leaves and the scent of rain. I call it home.
